video_title: Peter Mintzberg: Evolution of Digital Assets at Grayscale
transcript: [music] [music] Peter, great to see you. >> Yeah, it's pleasure. Thank you for having me. >> Why don't you take me back to your background that led to you coming into this world? >> Yeah, so uh on a personal basis, I'm originally from Brazil. Grew up there um and situations like hyperinflation. I have this memory of actually going to the supermarket with my mom in the morning because the prices were actually cheaper than in the afternoon. Talk about currency debasement. Um you know, and if I were to connect the dots backwards today, I think that's probably why I ended up having a career in asset and wealth management. It took me a few years to realize and connect the dots, but uh the experience with current currency debasement, the experience with hyperinflation, the experience with confiscation of assets by the government was uh quite uh intense growing up in Brazil. >> Yeah, so after you have that experience, how'd you get involved in the work world finance? >> Yeah, so I my career has been almost entirely in asset and wealth management. Uh I came to Grayscale from uh Goldman Sachs and before that I was at Apollo and BlackRock. And I always did the same thing. It was strategy and M&A. In that job, you're primarily looking for tailwinds in the marketplace, future tailwinds, so you can position the asset manager for growth. And that's half of the battle, I think, in asset management, finding the current currents and positioning the company to serve them well. 3 years ago, it was very clear to me that digital assets was going to be the next wave of growth in asset management and I wanted to be part of it, so I decided to join Grayscale. >> So before we jump into that decision, those are big steps at BlackRock, Apollo, Goldman, and Strategy. Would love to hear some of what you did and what you learned. >> Yeah, so um I >> a combination of strategy and M&A. So my last job before coming here was head of M&A and head of strategy for asset and wealth management. So it was a combination of um identifying trends, positioning the asset manager to serve them, and then executing on it both organically in some cases inorganically. When inorganically, the job was to find interesting opportunities and then go execute on that. So I suppose the biggest difference versus a banker is that I had to live with the results of my work and that gave me even more perspective in terms of selecting the deals that I wanted to work on and executing on them. >> What were some of the strategy initiatives that you pursued in each of those steps? >> Oh, I've done it all. Um, you know, several years of it in in three big organizations, but it ranged from blue sky strategy, which is "let's find a business we're not in and get into that and how do we do that," all the way to the more standard corporate strategy planning what are we going to do next year, what would be the priorities, and so forth, um and any everything in between. Uh if you ask about strategy and asset management, I've done it all. >> What did you find works well in that seat in any of the initiatives you're pursuing? >> I'll tell you what doesn't work well and and as a result what I learned from it. Um the typical ivory tower type of strategy where you sit down and you look at big uh flows and you project them on the forward and you try to then draw conclusions from it. It sounds nice, but it doesn't work as well as the second approach, which is client based. So more often than not, clients will tell us what they want and what they're missing and that's usually a better starting point than top down for strategy and asset management. >> So take me back a couple of years. You're sitting in this big strategy seat at Goldman and you make the decision that digital assets is the next wave. Not a new thing two, three years ago or as new as it's been. What was that decision process? >> It was easy. So, um I would say I did not leave traditional finance. I moved to where traditional finance was going. And you know, it was very clear that the same way you saw transformation in asset and wealth management over time with first with mutual funds at pooled investment vehicles offering benefits to clients that didn't exist before. Eventually ETFs came to fore with intraday liquidity, lower fees, transparency, all that stuff. Then we saw private capital coming to fore as well with idiosyncratic to returns and lower correlation and all that other stuff. And for me, digital assets is the next step of the natural evolution of asset and wealth management as opposed to a separate thing. >> What did you see in the timing of sort of what's happened with the digital asset world over the last couple of years that told you that now is the time to make the move? >> been transformational. Um I would say the last couple years we saw more change than in the last 10 years for the asset class. I'll give you an an anecdote. When I got here two years ago, if I were to call um a wealth platform or a financial advisor, I'll be probably like my call was blocked and I'll put on the spam list uh on their phone. You fast forward maybe 14 months and now we have hundreds and hundreds of inbound calls. We actually have today um a big problem which is we have more calls and interest than hours in the day to deal with them. So, it's been uh an incredible 180 degrees change, more than what I ever seen in in my career. >> As you look at that core thesis of why people are calling, you started with your experience in Brazil and the problems with hyperinflation, what's the reason why people are getting more interested in digital assets? >> I think uh there are different people with different interests. So you know, first and foremost, uh it's been a very well performing asset class over the long term. There's no question there is volatility, but we believe the returns are commensurable with volatility there. So that attracts a lot of people as you know, think about equities forecast today, probably in the mid single percentage points of returns and fixed income on a real basis, you're lucky if you're making any money. So there's no combination of five and one that gives you the seven that most investors are looking for. People are going up up into the right in the risk return curve and things like illiquids and private and digital assets is part of that movement. I think that's a big a big trend in investment. >> So take me back to Grayscale as a platform and walk me through the history of the business and where it is today. >> Yeah, so so Grayscale has been a pioneer in digital assets. Uh the firm has about 13 years of experience of track record which I'm told translates to 100 years in traditional finance. Starting all the way back in 13 with first publicly traded Bitcoin fund, the first publicly traded Ethereum fund like a few months later, all the way to more recently the first ETF that holds multiple tokens, staking ETFs. We have the highest, the broadest and largest range of ETFs that offer staking. So um it's a long history of innovation. There's a major innovation in our history and every year of our existence. >> The biggest change over the last couple years has been this movement to the ETF and there was the original Grayscale trust that was the one way that the wealth advisors could access Bitcoin in particular. What's happened in that transition from a trust to an ETF for Grayscale? >> So what really happened at that point in time uh was the entry of incredibly large, well-established asset managers into this space. We all know who they are, very credible, very high-quality institutions, which had two effects. One, it created more competition in a space that, like you said, Grayscale was was basically alone. And second, and very importantly, it de-risked the asset class because many investors saw these names they've been working with for, you know, 20 plus years, and hey, they are validating the asset class now. So we saw more competition and we saw also more market growth. So the pie got bigger even though there is more people playing it right now. >> And where does that stand today? >> In terms of market position. So we have been in direct competition with all these large players now for over two years. And if you were to do a mark-to-market to yesterday night or today this morning, we have the number one market share in every market where we compete on a market share of revenues basis. We have also the highest organic growth rate across the board when on these growth products that we we have been launching since conversion. And our margins are also very healthy. I think you know, I haven't done the full this is not US GAAP, but from what I can see, we have top of the of the league table margin. So I think we're doing okay. And it's a source of pride for all of us at Grayscale to be competing with these giants out there and getting these results that we're getting considering that we have 130 employees. >> How did you think about the strategic side of pricing? Because some of these big players come in and decidedly want to be the low-cost provider in the space. And you were coming from a position where being the only product, it was much more expensive to put it together than it would be in an ETF. >> So we >> address pricing in a combination of different ways. So you're probably referring more to Bitcoin and maybe Ethereum as well with GBTC and ETH. So we have a BTC ETF and we have an ETH ETF. We have four ETFs covering Bitcoin and Ethereum. And the rationale there is for clients that want tactical exposure to Bitcoin or Ethereum and are more concerned about the size of the ETF, the trading of that ETF, um and are not holding that for the long term. We have products for them, the GBTC and and ET ET products. Uh for clients that want to buy and hold, so they are more concerned about the total fees and not as much about liquidity, not as much about size of the ETF. It's kind of a buy and hold strategy minimizing management fees. We offer BTC and ETH. And that has worked incredibly well for us. Um um we reached an AUM level with BTC that was incredibly uh high. Now it's one of the top performing products across all digital assets and the same is true with ETH. >> What has been challenging in the transition to the ETF world in the last couple of years? >> The challenges we had before worked twofold. One was access for clients and two was education. [gasps] When we converted and Grayscale led the the conversion into ETPs or ETFs for digital assets, um the access problem was largely solved. The challenge that still exists is education. We've been investing enormous amount of time on it. So, for example, we've done road shows with hundreds and hundreds of financial advisors helping them understand what is this asset class about, um what kind of a risk profile the products have. It's not for everybody given the volatility. So where does it go and what does it make sense, what it doesn't? How do you actually manage the volatility of the of the portfolio if you incorporate into your clients book and so forth. I think there's a lot of work to be done there. It's getting much better, but it's the type of work that is going to take a long time to really establish itself. >> Have you thought about the products that you want to offer beyond just Bitcoin and Ethereum? >> Yeah, so we have today the what I believe is the broadest product platform in digital assets. We've over 40 tokens represented. Um we believe there are 40 million tokens out there. so in a way we've been selective is one in a million. Um and look most of them in our opinion are not investable. They are not representative of anything we want our clients to put money on. But you know there are interesting tokens out there. We found 40 of them so far and we follow a dual process to identify them. So there is a for lack of a better sentence a traditional finance type of screening where we're looking of like you know competitive environment this token is in what is the management team associated with that um etc etc. And there is also known chain analytics review. So we look at the governments governance. We look at the tokenomics the economics of that token. Um we look even programming language and we look how differentiated it is and so forth. The combination of both leads us to the products we believe are compelling enough to be to be launched. >> If you look at the 40 tokens that you've created products for walk me through some of the breadth of the projects that they're working on. >> It's across the board. So that's a misconception sometimes we have with first conversations with clients. They say look I want to allocate to digital assets. Maybe I'll buy Bitcoin and be done with, and what we tell them is, "Look, you might want to work a little bit harder on this and do due diligence with us, the same way, you would not want to own a sector of the S&P 500 only, you don't want to own just one token and they represent multiple different things. So we have um decentralized AI tokens, we have privacy tokens, we have Bitcoin. Uh and I can go on and on. Each one of these four they represent a different ecosystem, a different economic foundation, different trends in the marketplace. So you really have to double click and understand what you're investing in. And that's why I think clients appreciate working with us, a specialist as opposed to a broad-based asset manager because that's all we do. We wake up every day in the morning to think about these things and that's all we do. >> As you look at the underlying activity in tokens over the last couple years with with all of the interest in AI, you don't hear as much day-to-day about everything that's happening in the blockchain ecosystems. We'd love to hear some of what has been happening underneath the covers. >> Oh, there's a ton happening. It ranges that we're seeing like for the first time in in in years we've seen real applications going mainstream, whether is uh stable coins, uh tokenization is picking up as everybody knows. Um we have exchanges uh like Hyperliquid that run on blockchain and are growing very fast. Uh we have about 40% of Fortune 500 companies declaring they're actively working on blockchain initiatives to increase efficiency. There is a lot of innovation going on underneath the cover and there is also things that have been around for a while that are now resurfacing. One example is Zcash. Zcash is you can think of it as a Bitcoin-like product but with privacy features. And as people realize that everything you do on blockchain is public, um it becomes it calls the question how you get privacy. So people usually, let's say you're going to pay uh do payroll on Bitcoin and suddenly all salaries can be, you know, public. Not not everybody wants that. So Zcash he has very similar features to to Bitcoin in sense of constrained supply and a certain number of tokens and and and but it does have privacy options. We launched a Zcash ETF just a few days ago and it grew to over $700 million of AUM and maybe a couple weeks. That shows you that even things that have been around now for Zcash has been around for a few years are resurfacing based on new trends in the marketplace, which I find fascinating. >> Yeah. What are some other examples of of things like that that are really getting a lot of traction? >> Hyperliquid is getting a lot of traction. I alluded to it before. It's very interesting because Hyperliquid is a decentralized exchange. If you don't pay attention, you might not know that it runs on blockchain. Blockchain is the infrastructure that we run that runs and it grew very fast and last time I checked they had about 11 employees. So that got a lot of people's attention and Hyperliquid is the token that represents the economics of that exchange. Another product we launched recently and grew like to over $100 million very quickly. >> Have you thought about delivering as I say the difference between a beta in the space and selection of securities or alpha in the space? >> From a portfolio construction or tactics perspective, I would say today the market is primarily index. There are active plays out there, but I don't think that the Blackstone of digital assets has been created yet. It's something we're working very hard at Grayscale. We plan on launching our first active products sometime in the next few quarters. We've been making investments. We want to be very disciplined and rigorous about it. I do believe that there is more alpha opportunity today in digital assets than in say public equities. It feels a little bit like how the stock market used to be that if you do your research and you travel and visit the factory and you actually talk to the CEOs, you can actually develop a view and create alpha based on that view. Um that that's where digital assets are today and we want to be able to um offer that to our clients. >> How does the regulatory regime which we've now had some bottleneck in um in government towards the Clarity Act like play out and how does it affect what you're doing? >> The regulatory regime is critical um but if you actually take a step back from the setback of of the Clarity Act um I tell people we live today in the most favorable regulatory outlook for disaster class ever. So it's important to keep perspective on that compared to what existed say three or four years ago um these are the good times. These are the times where innovation is supported by by by by the environment we're in where innovation is in the US. We're launching products we're we you know we're developing the business um you would be better to have the Clarity Act so we can ensure that the current situation is sustainable over the long term. But as you saw just like an hour ago the SEC issued the new rule on on tokenization and I think the SEC and the CFTC will do their job in terms of ensuring innovation is happening in the US and uh all the entrepreneurs are supported and the clients are protected at the same time. And hopefully over time this can be codified in a way that gives people more of a sense of sustainability over the long term. >> As you put on your strategy hat in this seat how do you think about where all this heads the next couple of years and how you want to participate in it? >> I think all the change we've seen in the last two three years that we just went through um I think you'll pay you in comparison with the next two or three years. I think we're going to see 10 20 x more change in the next two three years. And the reason for that primarily is this two big trends that we've seen so far of AI and tokenization, which are still fairly incipient uh if you take a big picture perspective and have been operating almost independently are now converging. And no one knows really where this is going to be, but I think the exciting opportunities that come from this convergence are are are going to be transformative for our business and for the industry overall. >> So describe more about what is that convergence mean? >> So you think about tokenization from one side, which is most assets will be tokenized. What does that mean? It means that assets today that are only investable by a subset of clients become investable by mostly everybody. Second, assets that today are not investable can become investable as well. We talked about 40 million tokens. I think we might have 40 billion tokens sometime soon once everything becomes tokenized. On the other side, you have the AI. AI will help create portfolios of one. So um even if you go to a major warehouse today, more often than not you that they're going to risk assess you know your tolerance and and profile and you're going to find yourself in a certain model portfolio, right? Um um AI will be able to uh let us build a portfolio for you based on your needs, your plans for the future, etc. And it's not going to look like anyone else's portfolio. So the idea of this hyper customization for clients of exposures and the explosion of different types of investment opportunities, both will come together because there's no way a human being can intermediate this. I think it's really exciting. I think we're going to see a new uh set of asset managers uh coming into four. And um we're working very hard at Grayscale to be part of that business because at the end of the day, if I take a step back, Grayscale has been in the business of making things hard to invest investable. And we've been in the business of finding compelling investment opportunities in digital assets. That's that's where the world is going. The market in a way is coming to us, not the other way around. >> What do you see as uh next on the horizon of an asset that's been difficult to access that will become accessible through tokenization? >> The next uh immediate near term, and we're seeing some of it already, is exposure of US equities to international um investors in an easy format. I think that is happening. I don't think we have landed on a specific format that will work yet, but a while on its way. We're going to see also uh illiquid exposures that are hard to get out becoming more liquid. I think this whole topic of liquid versus illiquid is going to disappear over time. Private credit, private equity, and so forth, infrastructure. And then beyond that is really depending on the limit is your imagination, right? We can actually securitize cash flows or people's incomes or buildings and so forth. And then there is the combination of all these into portfolios, which is going to be really interesting as well. >> So have you looked at the asset level? Several years ago, there was the beginning of part of a real estate asset would get tokenized or part of the ownership structure. What's happened with some of the tokenization of things that are thought of as illiquid today, real estate assets, certain businesses, certain partnerships, things like that? >> Private health funds did as well. I don't think they took off. I think they were a little ahead of their time. But now we're starting to see the market move in that direction. And and there's still a lot of work to do in terms of not only providing people access and building the portfolios, but education as well, similar to what we have done in ETFs. Um but it's definitely going that direction. >> How do you create the standardization required to get sort of horizontal scale in one of those verticals? >> Yeah, that is a key challenge with tokenization today because it seems like there's so many different companies launching their own tokens. I think that we're going to see uh something similar to an exchange there where whoever captures liquidity first will win and the others eventually will go away. But we're not there yet. >> When you're out talking to institutions about the high-level case for digital assets in their portfolio, what are the key points today that are resonating? >> So it's interesting. Like two years ago, it was like, why should I touch this? Why should I invest? The question has changed quite a bit, like how should I do it? Um not for everybody, but usually people are interested. Uh they understand that actually the question is not as much should I invest on this anymore, but you know, is 0% the right allocation to this? And that's the real the question that we try to answer with them. >> And so as people are laying out these different options, what are the pluses and minuses of the different ways people can participate? >> So a lot of people like the ETFs. That's how their business captured like tens of billions of dollars so quickly. Uh they like to see their portfolio in one place, first of all. Many people don't want the inconvenience of having now a separate login and a separate account and a separate exchange and uh people just want to have it centralized and easy. Financial advisors like the ability of doing planning, seeing the full picture in one place, tax loss harvesting, all that stuff becomes easier in in a format they're used uh to. Um and then from an exposure perspective, more often than not, clients would start with Bitcoin. They just heard about it. Their friends it, or someone in their family bought it. Eventually they start asking, okay, what's past that? And then we get into that discussion. Look, you're you own a sector of the S&P. It might not be a bad idea to consider a diversification across different elements of digital assets. People like Hyperliquid as I as I said, Zcash is something that people are highly interested as well. Um so it really depends on the investor. We have um subset of of our clients that have been with us for 13 years and they bought BTC early. They're sitting on 400x returns. So they're more used to the asset class. So they are a little bit up into the right in the risk return curve. Tell me tell me about incipient tokens that have the potential to get market traction over the long term. >> Early on it felt like tokens could go everywhere. In the last couple of years it's maybe narrowed to financial use cases for the most part. I mean you still have a helium and things like that that that are beyond that. What are you seeing in the the breadth of ways that tokens are coming both into the financial services ecosystem and then outside of it? >> I would say most of what we do here is related to the financial system. Um we like investable tokens because that's the business that we're in. And that's what our focus is today. Um we don't tend to work on on on tokens that we can't um offer to our clients. >> When you put on your strategy hat here at Grayscale, what are the initiatives that you're looking to pursue going forward? >> So a big push for us is active management. We think there is alpha left um in in digital assets compared to like I said, public equities. We want to build that. There's a big build, but we're not doing it back to your original question on what works in strategy, what doesn't. Uh we're not doing it from an ivory tower type of perspective. Our clients are asking us for active strategies. So we're doing it based on their demand. >> How have you built the organization to support the increase in demand? >> We actually have an incredibly lean organization. So we're running about 40 different tokens with close to $20 billion of AUM with 130 people. And that includes multiple wrappers, multiple channels we serve from individuals directly all the way to sovereign wealth funds. And we are trying to build a new version of an asset manager that is AI first where we leverage distribution quite a bit based on marketing and communications. So the key governor of growth for us today is not the ability of the organization to to to launch products or to scale. It's more the number of hours in the day to actually push that through the system. >> How is AI working its way into your operations? >> It's working its way very fast. So like most companies, I think we have multiple types of engines running AI for us, the usual suspects. We are automating quite a bit of things. We're very careful with compliance and cybersecurity because of the business we're in. But you know, we have fully deployed it at this point and it's already proving some efficiencies, particularly around operations for us. >> What are some of the ways that AI have really enhanced the operations? >> It's been helpful for us on some processes that were manual before. So we keep now the humans at the end of the process to triple check everything because you know, we we have a fiduciary responsibility and I don't think AI is there yet. >> So as you now look a couple years in the seat, what is consistent with what you thought coming in and what's been a little different? >> Everything >> is different. Uh one of the one of the benefits of being um in this new asset class is things change every day. So as I was walking into this podcast, I just saw the news the SEC just just issued a positive there's a positive development on tokenization. There are news like literally every two hours. Uh it's it keeps it very interesting. It keeps it intellectually exciting. Um and I tell my team all the time that, you know, uh change is coming to us whether we want it or not might as well embrace it. >> So what's on the next frontier for Grayscale? >> Our aspiration is is large. Um we think that we have a dominant position today as a crypto native index asset manager. We want to build the active side of it, so the other leg and offer clients end-to-end solutions across the risk return return spectrum on digital assets. >> What would make this a success a couple of years from now? >> We are already uh as I mentioned to you like we're fortunate to be in a strong position. We are number one in every market where we compete on a market share of revenues basis. Um so um we want to extend that into active. We want to extend our reach internationally. Most of what we do today is domestic US. And um if we get both right, I think we're going to be in an even better position than today. >> Is it surprising to you that most of it is domestic given your history with hyperinflation and how that's happened in more countries outside the US than than in the US over time? >> That's how the company grew up. Um and frankly, we've have had so much demand, so many opportunities in the US which is still the biggest market in the world that it has kept us busy uh so far. But there is no question that there is a ton of opportunity in Latin America, Asia Pac, and Europe. And that's uh a part of our planning. >> Well, Peter, I want to make sure I get a chance to ask you a couple closing questions. What was your first paid job and what did you learn from it? >> My first paid job was probably 11 or 12 and it was in a toy store. And I was in charge of demonstrating the Rubik's Cube. Uh and uh that was the first wave of the Rubik's Cube in Brazil. And I wasn't there to to teach people how to solve it. I was there to demonstrate that it could be solved. Um uh interestingly, I was paid in toys, which was the best possible thing for at my you know, as an 11 or 12 years old in a toy store. Um now that was my first job. >> What did you take away from it? >> I learned that I like puzzles quite a bit. And honestly, uh since then I've been uh working on puzzles. The puzzles just get more complicated and multi-dimensional. They're not three-dimensional anymore. Um but uh you know, business is a big puzzle and we need to put the pieces together. That's what I do. >> What's the best advice you've ever received? >> Dream big, don't dream small. It's almost the same work uh to the one versus the other. And that came from a private equity investor that sponsored my education, my uh my coming to the US. And in in the the context of that is uh Brazil was a place where, you know, from at least in my circle, your your aspiration was to get like a stable job and just go about your life. Um and this guy was operating in the same environment and he said, look, you got to set your aspiration very high and work work backwards from there. And he worked for him. He um eventually built the biggest brewery in the world, bought Burger King and Heinz along the way. Um and I think there's something about not being limited by the environment you're in, but actually setting your aspiration and then working backwards that I learned from him. >> All right, Peter, last one. What life lesson have you learned that you wish you knew a lot earlier in life? >> So I'm an engineer, and uh used to be that getting the right answer was all about doing the right math and getting to that exact answer. And over time, um not working in engineering, but in business, I learned that sometimes you got to use your intuition and get to the right decision or at least the most perfect decision you can with the limited data that you have. And that is entirely okay, and you can't be waiting for the perfect answer all the time. I learned this somewhere along the way, and I wish I had learned a little earlier. >> Peter, thanks for this great update on what's happening in the digital asset world. >> It's a pleasure, Ted. Thank you. [music]
